data.title: Stocks to watch: SIA, CapitaLand India Trust, First Resources
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Oct 16):

Singapore Airlines (SIA) : Passenger traffic rose 2.8 per cent year on year in September, supported by healthy demand across most regions, it said on Thursday. The group said it carried 3.5 million passengers during the month, up 3.7 per cent from a year earlier. Shares of SIA closed 0.8 per cent or S$0.05 lower at S$6.49 on Thursday, before the news.

CapitaLand India Trust (Clint) : The trust on Thursday announced the launch of a new data centre in Chennai with an investment of about 19.4 billion rupees (US$203.2 million). CapitaLand Data Centre Chennai 01, Clint’s first data-centre development in the state of Tamil Nadu, will have a gross power capacity of 53 megawatts when completed by the end of 2026. Units of Clint fell 1.1 per cent or S$0.01 to S$0.88 on Thursday, before the news.

First Resources : The Singapore-listed palm oil producer on Thursday said fires detected within its Indonesian palm oil concessions were largely caused by external blazes spreading across its boundaries. The response follows a report by The Straits Times citing a recent Greenpeace investigation, which named First Resources and Bumitama Agri among entities with concession areas registering haze source points. Shares of First Resources fell 3.3 per cent or S$0.14 to S$4.08 on Thursday, before the filing.

data.title: Issue 216: Singaporeâs multi-fuel bunkering bet; listed companies hazy on haze risk
data.description:
Energy transition

Managing the transition to a multi-fuel bunkering future

As Singapore plans for a multi-fuel future for the maritime sector, its challenge is to be both versatile and efficient so that it can defend its status as a bunkering hub in the coming decades.

That means building up capabilities for different fuels while investing strategically to ensure that supply and demand are closely matched.

Singapore Senior Minister of State for Transport Murali Pillai says that the country is exploring the use of liquefied biomethane as a marine fuel, alongside plans to conduct its first ethanol bunkering operation and the release of guidelines for ammonia bunkering. Singapore is also expanding capacity for liquefied natural gas (LNG).

One of the maritime industry’s biggest decarbonisation challenges is how to replace the fossil-based marine fuel that powers vessels with greener alternatives. LNG, ethanol, methanol, methane and ammonia are among the leading candidates, while old classics like wind have also been incorporated into some modern designs.

Murali’s declarations, made at the Singapore International Bunkering Conference, reflect a bet that there will not be a single winner out of those alternatives.

Indeed, a recent analysis by the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) – an international think tank based in Singapore with funding support from industry and the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore – looks at different scenarios for the maritime fuel transition and none of them lead to a single dominant fuel by 2050.

“The future fuel landscape remains fragmented across all fuel types and in bunkering locations,” GCMD says in its report. “Shipowners that lock into a single fuel pathway today risk assets stranded by regulatory or cost outcomes.”

GCMD identifies four key signposts that affect uptake of alternative fuels:

The levelised cost of hydrogen is a primary determinant of the cost for low-carbon methanol and ammonia;

The cost of carbon dioxide obtained from biomass, which affects the cost of bio-methanol;

The cost trajectory of bio-methanol, which can be used in the near term and provide a bridge to greener electro-methanol in the longer term. Electro-methanol is produced using green hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide.

Regulatory treatment of ethanol in fuels based on food crops, which has a “binary” impact on ethanol’s penetration in marine fuels.

The cost and carbon footprint of the different fuels also varies depending on available resources, which can vary by region. GCMD expects that bio-methanol will be “cheapest along global sea lanes, with Asia being the most cost-competitive”.

Ammonia bunkering will be more likely along Asia sea lanes due to low production costs in China and India, while bio-ethanol will be linked to US supply chains due to low American production costs.

Because there is so much uncertainty around those factors right now, ship owners are increasingly ordering dual-fuel vessels that can use existing marine fuels as well as one of the alternatives. However, since there is no single dual-fuel combination dominating the orders, different fuel mixes will likely be required for many years after these vessels are built.

Data compiled by the World Shipping Council shows that 94 per cent of vehicle carrier orders and 78 per cent of container ship orders by deadweight tonnage are for dual-fuel ships as of March 2026. There were 440 dual-fuel vehicle carriers and container ships on the water at the time of the data, and 764 on order.

Most of the dual-fuel container vessels on order are for conventional-and-methane and conventional-and-methanol engines. There is one container ship on order with ammonia capability.

It’s not hard to see why Singapore is taking a multi-fuel approach under these circumstances. If Singapore is to remain a bunkering hub, it will need to cater for the different potential fuel types in the pipeline.

But actually building the infrastructure and supply chains to provide multiple fuels can be costly, which makes it important to time investments and expenditures to match demand. At the moment, the vast majority of dual-fuel engines are still running on conventional fuel.

GCMD explains that conventional fuel is still significantly cheaper than low-carbon alternatives at the moment, which means that most dual-fuel vessels are still not switching.

The economics could change and green alternatives could become cost-competitive if emissions were taxed aggressively enough, GCMD says. The maritime sector is considering the possibility of imposing a US$700 per tonne of greenhouse gas emissions penalty under a proposed net zero framework, but international consensus is missing. The industry could make a decision in December at a meeting of the Marine Environment Protection Committee.

Amid that uncertainty, being too aggressive on building out infrastructure for alternative fuels when demand is still absent might make it difficult to recover costs, which would make it more difficult to maintain a commercially sustainable bunkering hub.

Singapore manages that risk by focusing on capability building for now. For instance, Singapore has developed a technical reference for ammonia bunkering, and is carrying out pilot bunkering trials for different fuels. The aim is to start building the software now to shorten the time to delivery when the need arises.

The economic and logistical realities of producing low-carbon fuel for ships means that green bunkering in the future will comprise a more heterogeneous landscape than the conventional marine fuel system we have today. But knowing what the end state might look like is only one part of the challenge; navigating the transition is the other, just as important part.

Climate risk

Risk disclosures on haze need more visibility

Singapore-listed companies may need to give more deliberate consideration to the haze as a risk to be managed, and assure investors of those considerations.

The prolonged season of the transboundary air pollution currently besieging Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia has disrupted a swathe of activities. For example, the haze has led to severe curtailment of outdoor activities and suspended flights.

Of course, this is not the first time that South-east Asia has encountered the haze, with the severe outbreak in 2013 leading to the enactment of Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act. In fact, Singapore is so familiar with the haze that it has well-established guidelines on when pollution levels are unhealthy and the appropriate health and safety responses at those levels.

Yet many listed companies’ disclosures do not seem to directly address the risk posed by the haze, even for companies that would seem to be more exposed to such risk.

For instance, theme park developer Sim Leisure Group’s sustainability report identifies extreme weather as a material physical climate risk, but only considers that risk in the form of extreme rainfall and increased flooding. The bulk of the company’s revenues are from Malaysia and Singapore, where haze conditions pose an ongoing threat to guest numbers as well as worker health and safety at its outdoor theme parks.

ISOTeam, a building maintenance and estate upgrading group with a leading presence in building painting works, performs substantial work outdoors. Its climate-related disclosures discuss heatwaves, water stress and sea level rise as key physical climate risks. There is no mention of the haze.

Investors might be concerned that a company deems sea level rise, which may only manifest at a serious enough level many years into the future, important enough to disclose but not the haze, which occurs almost every year at varying levels of severity.

This is not to suggest that companies have not been dealing with the haze. In fact, both of the mentioned companies have been around long enough to be familiar with serious haze events of past years.

But leaving the haze out of disclosures can create a gap in investors’ appreciation of how a company manages climate risk, and raise questions about the thoroughness of a company’s assessment of climate risks. This is increasingly relevant with rising temperatures expected to raise the severity and frequency of serious haze events, even if human activities are still a major underlying cause of the haze.

The haze is also a reminder that companies need to be especially conscientious when it comes to assessing their exposure to climate risk, and not overly rely on convenient boilerplate risks. One of the biggest dangers of climate change is unpredictability, so prudent companies should be assessing the exposure of various aspects of their businesses in detail.

  • Singapore’s low-carbon electricity 2035 target is ‘aspirational’: EMA

data.title: 2026 BMW i7 review: Buyers of BMWâs flagship have one surprising trait
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] If you want to watch a BMW employee squirm, ask them why the 7 Series has such a gargoyle face, then sit back and watch as they issue a spluttering protest to the contrary.

The honest answer, I suspect, is that the brand’s flagship car was never meant to be pretty or graceful, but imposing and provocative.

So maybe it says something that the mid-life facelift (or Life Cycle Impulse, or LCI, to use a BMW marketing term) for the latest 7 (codenamed G70) was unusually thorough.

In addition to new bumpers and lights, BMW gave it a reshaped bonnet and something of a nosejob that slimmed down and sharpened its grille. The result is neater and better looking, without being any less provocative or brooding.

While I wouldn’t call the G70 LCI a stunner now, it does look like it rolled out of the Dark Deco Gotham City of the 1990s Batman cartoon, with its monolithic slabs and glowing grille.

You can well imagine that the man behind the wheel has a secret cave stocked with weapons and a latex suit with a cowl.

The major makeover might imply that BMW was trying to fix something about the 7, but in truth, the car’s product team probably started on this facelift even before the G70’s launch in 2022.

By then, they would have known that BMW was about to pivot to the Neue Klasse (or “new class”) technology platform that provides the bones of the current iX3 and upcoming i3 Series, but couldn’t glom from it for the 7 Series in time.

Four years later, if the new i7 50 xDrive is anything to go by, the new 7 has borrowed as much as it could from the Neue Klasse cars.

Launched here solely in spicy M Sport trim, the pure electric limo gets BMW’s latest-generation battery cells, which stretch the claimed range to 728 km on a good day.

If you still want petrol power, a 3.0-litre turbo version, the 735, kicks off the range at S$684,888 with a Certificate of Entitlement.

You still press a Start button to wake up the i7, unlike the iX3’s get-in-and-go approach, and the brakes aren’t programmed for the same smooth stops as in the Neue Klasse cars, but you do get the snazzy display systems from the very newest BMWs.

That includes the Panoramic Vision Display – a strip of information along the base of the windscreen which looks gorgeous, keeps your eyes up near the road and stays crisply legible in all conditions.

The main touchscreen took me a while to work out, and since nearly every physical control has been purged, adjusting the air-conditioning means jabbing at glass.

For this I blame China, where buttons are apparently passe and big screens are a big deal (hence a new extra screen for the front passenger). At this price though, would it kill BMW to leave me a few knobs to twist, so I can see where my money went?

Another complaint: The glass roof warms up in the sun and radiates heat at your head, even with the roller shade drawn. At least the much-improved air-conditioning vents chill the cabin better. 

Still, driving the i7 50 made me forget its foibles because it’s still a class act underneath its passengers’ bums.

Air springs give it a pillowy ride, but when you’re feeling frisky you can engage Sport mode to lower the car so it hunkers down for fast corners, tackling them with a taut precision you don’t expect of a limousine.

Rear-axle steering, which turns the back wheels slightly, makes it surprisingly wieldy, too. And while many cars have turned harsh chasing sportiness, the envelope between plushness and agility here is impressively wide.

With 455 horsepower, the i7 50 lunges to 100 kmh in 5.5 seconds, but it feels quicker because it responds instantly to every twitch of your right foot.

It’s fast in an authoritative way, and it’s almost too quiet on the move; at a steady cruise the ears pick up a faint gearbox whine, because there’s little else to hear.

All this matters because, surprisingly, most 7 Series buyers here still prefer to do the driving themselves.

I suppose that makes sense, because as plush and roomy as it is in the back of the BMW, people who prefer to be driven can now tool around in lounge-on-wheels machines such as the Lexus LM or Zeekr 009.

That said, BMW’s own i5 is sharper to drive and not much less refined than the i7.

So why bother with a 7 Series?

Because it’s undeniably grand, it has presence and, with the owner behind the wheel, it signals both wealth and a certain self-deterministic world view.

It still isn’t pretty, but then nobody in Gotham admires the gargoyles, either. They’re just where the man in charge perches to look down on the city.

data.title: Ferrariâs S$2.1 million EV trips the light fantastic
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Diamonds are forever, but they might have some competition from Ferrari.

“Some 95 per cent of the cars we’ve produced since 1947 are still on the road today,” Emanuele Carando, Ferrari’s global head of product marketing, told The Business Times. “You will never scrap a Ferrari.”

The company is now hoping the Luce, its first electric car, will be no exception.

Needless to say, the sleek machine is completely unlike anything that has ever borne the brand’s prancing horse logo. Aside from being battery-powered, it is Ferrari’s first five-seater, with four doors and a 597-litre boot that Carando said would swallow several golf bags.

It costs S$2,093,306 without options or a Certificate Of Entitlement, around S$100,000 less than the Purosangue, the high-riding four-seater. That, too, was an unusual beast when it came out, but it at least has a high-revving V12 engine – the favourite layout of founder Enzo Ferrari.

“We didn’t want to make a copycat of what we already had,” Carando said of the Luce’s format. At the same time, he said Ferrari believes that electric propulsion offers the biggest advantage in a larger car like the Luce, which is Italian for “light”. For small two-seaters, combustion engines and hybrids remain the better answer, which rules out an electric berlinetta (or coupe) for now.

Carando called the car “an addition” rather than a transition, adding that Ferrari is “technologically neutral” and will keep building screaming engines for as long as regulations allow. Combustion fans, rejoice.

Yet, despite not having a traditional engine, the Luce feels like a Ferrari and serves up driving thrills like one, Carando insists.

“Whenever you think about a Ferrari, you think about a product which gives emotion. That’s the most important thing,” he said. “Sometimes when you drive an electric car, it’s like the car is driving you.”

To make the Luce more agile and feel glued to the road, engineers gave each wheel its own motor, plus actuators for steering and ride height. “It’s almost like having 12 motors,” Carando said.

Paddles behind the steering wheel select five levels of power on the right and five of regenerative braking on the left, without imitating gearshifts.

Ferrari estimates the Luce’s range at more than 530 km, and a fast enough charger can add 70 kWh, more than half the battery, in 20 minutes. The battery, motors and charging system carry an eight-year warranty, and key components were developed in-house by Ferrari, with expertise gained from Formula 1 racing.

The development team worked hard on giving the Luce a sonorous voice, as well. “We’ve been investing a lot in the sound, not making something fake,” Carando said, before playing a clip of Ferrari’s F1 drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc having a ball in a Luce, with a whirring wail in the background.

That sound comes from the hardware itself. A device on the rear axle amplifies the vibrations of the spinning motors, much like the pickup on an electric guitar. Carando compares the approach to a doctor using a stethoscope: you can’t hear your own heart, but it is beating in the background.

While the Luce’s performance means it could run with many Ferraris – a whopping 1,050 horsepower output means it accelerates to 100 kmh in 2.5 seconds and 200 kmh in only 6.8 – there are several new electric cars that are even more powerful. Shouldn’t a Ferrari be the best of the best, I put to him?

“How can you be the best of the best? Having the best target data, or having a car which drives the best?” he said. “Making a fast car, it’s easy, but is that what makes it fun to drive? We don’t believe so.”

“We do believe it’s much better to make a car which is extremely fun whenever you’re driving on a winding road. You just need to have a roundabout in order to understand, (the Luce is) an incredible car.”

Carando flew in from Ferrari’s hometown of Maranello to launch the Luce here on Monday (Oct 12), at a Good Class Bungalow that turned out to be a customer’s new home.

Few car makers can count on a buyer to lend them their house, but that is the kind of arrangement that makes having a Ferrari feel less like owning a car than joining a family.

The real test for the Luce won’t be how it performs according to a stopwatch, but whether it’s eventually seen as another diamond within the family jewels.

data.title: Palm oil stocks slide after Singapore begins looking into which firms responsible for haze
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Shares of palm oil producers fell on Friday (Oct 16) after Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that the country is looking into which companies may be responsible for haze-causing fires.

Where warranted, Singapore will take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries, said PM Wong in a Facebook post on Thursday.

First Resources shares fell as much as 9.1 per cent to S$3.71 at 9.20 am. The counter pared some losses to end the day 6.9 per cent lower at S$3.80.

Bumitama Agri retreated 7.5 per cent to an intraday low of S$1.73, then rebounded somewhat to close 4.8 per cent lower at S$1.78. Golden Agri-Resources dropped as much as 3.4 per cent to S$0.28.

The Straits Times reported on Thursday that a recent Greenpeace investigation had named First Resources and Bumitama Agri among entities with concession areas registering haze source points.

First Resources on Thursday defended itself, stating that fires detected within its Indonesian palm oil concessions were largely caused by external blazes spreading across its boundaries. It attributed the elevated fire risk in West Kalimantan to a “severe” El Nino-induced drought. Indonesia on Thursday blamed peatland degradation by past food estates for its worst wildfire season in 11 years, and said it will work to restore its peat ecosystem.

Air quality deteriorated across all of Singapore overnight. The 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index reading in the central region hit the “very unhealthy” level at midnight on Friday and stood at 227 at 9 am – a new high for the year. Readings in the rest of the country were at the “unhealthy” level.

Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu on Wednesday said that Singapore was “keeping its options open” on whether it will take action against errant companies under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.

That followed a National Environment Agency spokesperson saying that the agency “has been closely monitoring the haze situation, gathering information on fire hot spots, their sources and impact on Singapore’s air quality”.

data.title: US manufacturing output rises in September
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] US factory production increased in September, but lost considerable momentum in the third quarter amid headwinds from the Middle East conflict, which has snarled supply chains and raised energy prices.

Manufacturing output rebounded 0.3 per cent in September following a revised 0.2 per cent decline in August, the Federal Reserve said on Friday (Oct 16).

The rise was in line with economists’ expectations.

Factory production was previously estimated to have dropped 0.3 per cent in August. Output advanced 1.1 per cent on a year-over-year basis in September.

It grew at a 0.7 per cent annualised rate in the third quarter after accelerating at a 5.6 per cent pace in the second quarter.

Manufacturing accounts for about 9.4 per cent of the economy.

While an artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out and businesses rebuilding inventories to meet robust domestic demand are supporting factory activity, higher energy prices, a trade war with Canada and rising borrowing costs pose downside risks to production.

Diesel prices have surged to a record high as the US-Israel war with Iran drags on, and economists said the economy could soon feel the effects through higher prices for goods, including at the supermarket, which could weigh on demand.

Durable goods manufacturing production edged up 0.1 per cent, lifted by gains in the output of primary metals, machinery and electrical equipment, appliances and components.

Production of motor vehicles and parts fell 3 per cent. Durable goods manufacturing output increased at a 3.8 per cent rate in the third quarter, partly boosted by a 28.4 per cent surge in the production of semiconductors and related electronic components related to the AI spending boom.

Non-durable manufacturing production rose 0.4 per cent over the month amid gains in printing and chemicals output. Non-durable manufacturing output, however, fell 1.6 per cent last quarter.

Mining production rose 0.2 per cent in September and grew at a 5 per cent rate in the July-to-September quarter. Utilities jumped 3.5 per cent amid demand for air-conditioning. Their output increased at a 14.8 per cent pace in the third quarter.

Overall industrial production rose 0.7 per cent in September after gaining 0.1 per cent in August. Industrial output increased 2.2 per cent year on year in September. It advanced at a 2.8 per cent pace in the third quarter after growing at a 4.8 per cent rate in the second quarter.

Capacity utilisation for the industrial sector, a measure of how fully companies are using their resources, rose to 76.9 per cent in September from 76.4 per cent in August.

It is 2.5 percentage points below its 1972-to-2025 average. The operating rate for the manufacturing sector edged up to 75.9 per cent from 75.8 per cent in August. It is 2.3 percentage points below its long-run average. REUTERS

data.title: MOE to consider closing schools, O-level exams may be postponed if haze turns hazardous: Desmond Lee
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Schools will remain open and students will take their O- and A-Level exams in enclosed, air-conditioned venues with air purifiers.

Education Minister Desmond Lee said on Oct 16 that the ministry wants to minimise disruption for students, who have been working hard to prepare for their national exams. Written papers for O-levels start on Oct 19 and practical A-level exams are ongoing.

Speaking at the haze task force’s press conference on Oct 16, Lee said the Ministry of Education will consider rescheduling O-level papers in line with the health advisory for younger students, should the PSI forecast reach hazardous levels, denoted by readings exceeding 300. The Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) is a measure of air quality here.

The A-level papers are generally less likely to be affected, he said, as the students are older. But the ministry will also take into account actual circumstances in deciding whether examinations should proceed, he said.

Should students feel unwell and are unable to take or continue with an exam, they should see a doctor, get a medical certificate, and apply for special consideration through their schools, Lee said. Schools will guide these students on the necessary procedure.

Any affected papers will be rescheduled to the earliest practicable date, with the Singapore Examinations and Assessment Board (SEAB) announcing the changes publicly, he added.

Schools will inform students and parents directly if any national exam needs to be rescheduled, he said. Lee cautioned against misinformation about school closures circulating on social media.

“Now there have also been circumstances where fake news about school closures has been put out on social media, causing confusion and anxiety,” he said, urging parents, students and the public to refer to MOE’s official channels and Parents Gateway for updates.

More information about any changes in the scheduling of O- and A-level examinations will be available on the SEAB website, he added.

The main written papers for the GCE O-Level examinations are scheduled to begin on Oct 19 and run until Nov 10. The GCE A-Level examinations are ongoing, with H2 Physics and Biology practical examinations scheduled for Oct 19 and 22 respectively, ahead of the main written papers starting on Nov 2 with General Paper.

All papers for 2026’s Primary School Leaving Examination concluded on Sep 30.

On Oct 16, Lee also outlined measures to keep schools operating amid worsening air quality, including adjustments to outdoor activities, the deployment of air purifiers and additional precautions for students with pre-existing health conditions.

For younger students, MOE will consider closing schools and moving to home-based learning from pre-school to secondary school levels if the 24-hour PSI forecast for the following day reaches the hazardous range of 301 and above, he said.

Lee said parents and guardians will also be strongly encouraged to keep infants and young children at home in such a scenario, given their greater vulnerability to the health effects of haze.

Kindergarten programmes and early intervention services for children with developmental needs will also be suspended under such circumstances, he said.

These include the Early Intervention Programme for Infants and Children (EIPIC and EIPIC-P) services, and pre-school-based early intervention programmes, such as the Development Support-Plus programme and Development Support-Learning Support programme.

Lee acknowledged that this can be challenging for parents who cannot work from home or find alternative care for their children.

Therefore, MOE Kindergartens and Kindergarten Care as well as pre-schools licensed under the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) will remain physically open, he noted.

Children who report to these facilities will be able to participate in indoor activities, such as reading and hands-on activities, with precautions such as the use of air purifiers in enclosed rooms, he added.

Lee also reassured the public that primary and secondary schools, student care centres and special student care centres will remain physically open to take care of students who do not have alternative care arrangements.

In-person lessons in junior colleges and other post-secondary institutions such as polytechnics and universities would likely continue as students are older, although adjustments may be made depending on actual circumstances, he said.

Asked when primary schools would switch to home-based learning, Lee said the ministry would consider doing so when the PSI forecast reaches the hazardous range, though it is “not rigidly wedded to numbers”.

Decisions would also take into account other factors, including students’ ages, vulnerabilities and pre-existing health conditions, he said.

Schools also have the autonomy to adjust precautions based on students’ needs, as they are best placed to assess the situation on the ground, he said.

Any decision to shift to home-based learning would generally be made a day in advance, Lee said, based on the National Environment Agency’s PSI forecast, to give schools time to prepare.

The situation varies across schools, said Lee, when asked if more students have taken medical leave and whether this would be taken into account when deciding whether to switch to home-based learning even if air quality does not reach hazardous levels.

Some schools saw no difference in student illness rates compared with the same period in 2025, while others reported more students falling ill, he said.

Schools are prepared for home-based learning if needed, he added, drawing on experience gained during the Covid-19 pandemic, when disruptions to classroom learning were more prolonged and uncertain. “We keep the muscles warm over the years, and if there is a need to do so, we will do so.”

During the severe haze episode in September 2015, MOE closed all primary and secondary schools for a day on Sep 25 that year, when air quality was forecast to reach very unhealthy or potentially hazardous levels. An O-Level practical examination originally scheduled for that day was postponed to Sep 29.

The PSLE, however, proceeded as scheduled on Oct 1 that year, with candidates taking their papers in enclosed spaces equipped with air purifiers. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Bank of America taps high-grade bond market after turbulent week
data.description:
[NORTH CAROLINA] The Bank of America (BOA) has kicked off the sale of investment-grade bonds, becoming the third major Wall Street company to tap a turbulent market this week after reporting third-quarter results.

The lender is marketing debt in as many as four parts, ranging in maturity from three to 11 years, said a person with direct knowledge of the matter.

The longest tranche is initially being offered at a yield premium of about 1.2 percentage points to US Treasuries, the person added, who asked not to be identified because they are not authorised to speak publicly.

The unusual Friday offering comes after numerous companies held off on high-grade bond sales over the past few days, as Treasury yields swung sharply on stronger-than-expected inflation data and worries about the artificial-intelligence trade.

BOA was the only one of the six big Wall Street banks that did not tap the market in the third quarter, raising just US$17 billion so far this year, the least among the group. In its latest offering, it raised US$10 billion in April.

The six banks, which often time their borrowing to follow quarterly reports, are projected by Barclays to raise about US$41 billion through high-grade bond sales this quarter.

That is 30 per cent more than the average for the period since 2015. JPMorgan Chase and Morgan Stanley earlier this week raised a combined US$10 billion.

BOA shares slumped earlier this week after reporting third-quarter earnings that missed analyst projections, with both its stock and fixed-income tradings falling short of estimates.

The company’s bond sale is set to be just the fifth high-grade offering to price on a Friday this year, going by data compiled by Bloomberg. The last was a July offering from a Deere unit. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Deluge shares close 6.7% higher on first day of mainboard listing
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Shares of Deluge Corporation closed 6.7 per cent higher at the end of their first day of trading on the Singapore Exchange (SGX) mainboard on Friday (Oct 16), after the fire protection specialist’s initial public offering (IPO) was 3.86 times subscribed.

The shares opened at S$0.63, 5 per cent above the S$0.60 offer price, and then hit an intraday high of S$0.65 a share.

The closing share price of S$0.64 gave the company a market capitalisation of about S$92.8 million.

About 8.73 million shares changed hands on the debut trading day.

The IPO comprised 15.6 million shares at S$0.60 apiece, including 14.8 million placement shares and 800,000 shares for the public offer, Deluge said on Thursday.

The public offer was 11.97 times subscribed, with 327 valid applications for 9.53 million shares. Application monies amounted to about S$5.74 million.

The placement tranche was 3.42 times subscribed, attracting indications of interest for 50.63 million shares, worth about S$30.4 million. Investors included Lion Global Investors and UOB Asset Management.

Separately, cornerstone investors subscribed for 23.4 million new shares at the offer price, amounting to about S$14 million. They included Amova Asset Management Asia, Avanda Investment Management, HB Equity Partners and Whitefield Capital Management, alongside several individual investors.

The IPO and cornerstone tranche raised gross proceeds of about S$23.4 million. After listing expenses of S$3.27 million, Deluge expects net proceeds of about S$20.1 million.

The firm plans to use the proceeds to fund business expansion and working capital, strengthen its operational capabilities, and pursue strategic partnerships, acquisitions, joint ventures and regional expansion.

Lee Wai Wah, executive director and group chief executive of Deluge, said: “Our listing gives us a stronger platform to pursue larger projects and capture opportunities from Singapore’s continued infrastructure development.

“We intend to build on our experience to grow our project portfolio, while expanding our inspection, testing, maintenance and upgrading services as our installed base increases.”

Deluge had an order book of about S$433.04 million as at Sep 16, which it expects to fulfil primarily over the next four financial years.

Founded in 1983, the company provides fire detection and protection systems for critical infrastructure, including hospitals, airports, educational institutions and shopping malls. 

Its rail-related contracts include work on the Cross Island Line, the Tengah and Changi East depots, and the Rapid Transit System Link between Singapore and Johor Bahru.

Deluge is listed on the SGX mainboard under the stock code 9DC.

data.title: Nvidia-backed CoreWeave stock, bond set for weekly plunge as rate-hike fears hit AI bet
data.description:
COREWEAVE’S shares and bonds were set for steep weekly losses on Friday (Oct 16), underscoring investor worries over the cloud-computing company’s US$50 billion debt load that has rippled in the artificial intelligence industry.

The Nvidia-backed company came into focus this week after the latest inflation data boosted bets on interest-rate hikes, raising the chances of higher payout on borrowings by data-centre and AI-infrastructure companies with huge debt.

CoreWeave shares fell more than 6 per cent in early trading after tumbling over 15 per cent this week, their worst week in nearly two months.

“A hot inflation print triggered a sharp sell-off in CoreWeave because its business model is a highly indebted play on future data centre demand,” BCA Research analysts said.

“Although the rest of the tech complex is also sensitive to the pace and magnitude of AI adoption and use, it is, on average, considerably less sensitive to interest rates,” they added.

The sell-off is a stark reminder that AI companies’ reliance on debt is becoming a risk for investors, and punctures the notion that companies at the heart of the AI boom are immune to macroeconomic headwinds.

CoreWeave’s stock has already lost about a fifth of its value, or nearly 9.6 billion, so far in October.

Debt market jitters

The yield on CoreWeave’s October 2031 maturity US dollar bond briefly surged past 16 per cent on Thursday. It is set to decline for a fifth straight week, down about US$0.03 on the dollar this week.

The cost of insuring against CoreWeave’s debt has surged past 1,000 basis points to record highs this week, going by data from S&P Global Market Intelligence.

Investor worries over CoreWeave’s massive debt load and distressed bond yields had a contagion affect that impacted rival Nebius Group, the shares of which were set for their steepest weekly fall in two months.

Still, several analysts were not ready to throw in the towel. Evercore analysts maintained their outperform rating on CoreWeave stock.

“The markets appear to be extrapolating a higher secondary-market bond yield as evidence the business model has stopped working, which we don’t think is the case,” they wrote in a note.

Others argued the rout in CoreWeave should not be seen as a sign that the AI rally is coming to an end.

“You cannot take CoreWeave as the poster child for AI,” said Tommaso Leodari, chief investment officer at Dubai-based hedge fund Index & Cie. REUTERS
